Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting title: Northbridge Financial x Redwood Inference — Security review: Audit logs + SIEM export (Splunk)
Date: 2025-01-22
Start time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 47 min

Attendees
- Fatima Noor (Redwood) — Solutions Engineering (regulated customers)
- Marcus Lin (Redwood) — Security Engineering
- Naomi Feldman (Redwood) — PM, Security & Compliance
- Jenna Walsh (Northbridge) — Director, Security Operations
- Paul Nguyen (Northbridge) — Splunk Platform Engineer
- Ravi Iyer (Northbridge) — GRC / Compliance
- Marta Klein (Northbridge) — Enterprise Architect

Summary (auto-generated)
Northbridge asked detailed questions about Redwood’s audit logging and the upcoming SIEM-ready audit export (beta) including event coverage, retention, schema stability, delivery guarantees, encryption, tenant isolation, and Splunk HEC specifics (ACK, batching, error handling). Redwood confirmed audit export uses at-least-once delivery with durable buffering and retry/backoff, provides a versioned schema (v1) and recommends downstream dedupe using a stable event_id. Redwood will share the schema and Splunk setup guide, and coordinate beta enablement.

Topics (auto-generated)
- Audit event coverage and schema versioning
- SIEM export delivery semantics (at-least-once), duplicates, and dedupe guidance
- Splunk HEC connector details (ACK, batching limits, throttling)
- Retention and evidence (SOC 2 / ISO alignment)
- Filtering and noise/cost controls
- Operational visibility: health status, backlog, alerts, replay

Action items (auto-generated)
- Redwood to send Audit Event Schema v1 and Splunk HEC setup guide
- Northbridge to confirm Splunk endpoint/ACK requirements and parsing conventions
- Schedule follow-up to cover queries/dedupe patterns and pilot readiness

Transcript

[00:00] Fatima Noor: Alright, cool. We’re recording—this is the security review around audit logs and SIEM export. Thanks everyone for joining. Quick intros on our side, I’m Fatima, solutions engineering. I work with regulated customers.

[00:10] Marcus Lin: Hey, Marcus, security engineering. I’m one of the owners for audit logging and the export pipeline security controls.

[00:16] Naomi Feldman: Naomi here, PM for security and compliance features, including the SIEM-ready export that we’re in beta on.

[00:22] Jenna Walsh: Hi, Jenna, I run SecOps at Northbridge. Paul is our Splunk person. Ravi is GRC, and Marta is architecture.

[00:30] Paul Nguyen: Hey everyone.

[00:31] Ravi Iyer: Hello.

[00:33] Marta Klein: Hi.

[00:36] Fatima Noor: Great. Jenna, do you want to start with what you need out of this call? I know you had some questionnaire items but we can keep it conversational.

[00:44] Jenna Walsh: Yeah. We’re evaluating a few inference vendors—Bedrock, Azure OpenAI, and you folks. The sticking point for us is auditability. Specifically: can we get audit events into Splunk reliably, what’s the retention, and what are the guarantees. Also what’s in the events—like IP, actor, tenant, request IDs—and how stable is the schema.

[01:06] Fatima Noor: Yep, makes sense. The short version: we have platform audit logs today, and we’re rolling out “SIEM-ready audit export” which pushes audit events to Splunk HEC, Datadog logs, or S3. In beta we’re starting with those three sinks.

[01:20] Naomi Feldman: And just to set expectations: the export feature is gated by a feature flag and we’re onboarding a small set of enterprise design partners. Northbridge looks like a fit based on the requirements you shared.

[01:31] Jenna Walsh: Okay. Let’s dig in. Audit event coverage: what’s included? We care about admin actions, API key lifecycle, auth events, RBAC, and config changes. Also, like, model changes if that’s a thing.

[01:46] Marcus Lin: Totally. Our audit taxonomy is centered on “security-relevant actions.” In v1 schema we include authentication events (login success/fail, SSO events where applicable), credential events (API key created/rotated/revoked), RBAC changes (role assignments, permission changes), workspace/tenant changes, and audit export configuration changes—so enabling a destination, updating a token, changing filters—those are all auditable.

[02:10] Marcus Lin: For model lifecycle specifically, we log changes that affect serving configuration from the control plane—like pinning a model version for a workspace, changing routing policy, or changing an environment setting. We do not log every single inference request as an audit event. That’s a different class of telemetry.

[02:27] Marta Klein: That’s good actually. We don’t want every token.

[02:30] Jenna Walsh: Right, we don’t want to ingest high-volume junk. Okay, schema: can you tell us what fields we get? Specifically: who, what, where, when.

[02:41] Marcus Lin: Yep. At a high level each event has: event_id (a UUID), event_type, emitted_at timestamp, and a schema_version field. Then “actor” fields—actor_type (user, service, system), actor_id, and for users we include a stable user identifier and display name when available. Then “target” / “resource” fields: resource_type, resource_id, and sometimes resource_name. We include request_id / trace_id correlation IDs where we have them so you can tie to app logs.

[03:11] Marcus Lin: For “where,” we include source IP when the event is triggered via API or console, plus user agent if present. Geo is optional—we can provide region info derived from IP in some deployments, but we’re cautious there. For beta, we’re focusing on IP and region as optional fields and we’ll document when they are present.

[03:33] Ravi Iyer: On PII—what do you consider PII in these events, and do you redact?

[03:38] Marcus Lin: Good question. We follow a rule set: we don’t include prompt contents or model outputs. We avoid storing secrets. For user identifiers, we include user email only if the tenant has that in the identity profile, but we can configure to prefer immutable IDs. For IP addresses, we treat them as sensitive but typically acceptable in audit logs. If you require IP hashing or suppression we should talk—beta supports filtering but not per-field transforms.

[04:07] Jenna Walsh: We need IP addresses, frankly.

[04:10] Marcus Lin: That’s the common case.

[04:12] Paul Nguyen: From Splunk side, we care about parsing. Are these JSON events? Is there a “source” and “sourcetype” suggestion?

[04:20] Fatima Noor: The payload is JSON. For Splunk HEC, we send as HEC events with an event body that’s JSON. We’ll include recommended sourcetype in the guide, but you can override in your HEC input config. In the beta guide we propose something like sourcetype=redwood:audit and source=redwood-inference.

[04:39] Paul Nguyen: Okay. Now the big one: delivery guarantees. “Reliably export” can mean a lot. Is it exactly-once?

[04:47] Naomi Feldman: It’s at-least-once.

[04:48] Paul Nguyen: Okay so duplicates possible.

[04:51] Marcus Lin: Correct. We chose at-least-once because it’s the only way to give strong durability across sinks and transient network failures without creating correctness issues inside the vendor endpoints. We provide a stable event_id so you can dedupe.

[05:05] Jenna Walsh: What would cause duplicates? Retries?

[05:09] Marcus Lin: Exactly. For example: we send a batch to Splunk, Splunk returns a 5xx or the connection drops after ingest but before we receive a response. We retry. That can create duplicates downstream. Same story if HEC ACK is enabled and the ack doesn’t come back within the window.

[05:27] Paul Nguyen: Do you support HEC ACK?

[05:29] Fatima Noor: Yes, optional. If you enable HEC ACK on your side, we can use it. That gives you stronger confirmation that Splunk indexed the event, but it can add latency. We can tune it per destination.

[05:44] Paul Nguyen: We usually enable ACK for audit feeds. But we also have strict limits; if the ACK queue backs up, things get weird.

[05:53] Fatima Noor: Totally. That’s why we’ve got backoff and circuit-breaker behavior. If Splunk starts returning 429s or 5xx, we’ll back off, we’ll mark the destination degraded, and we’ll buffer.

[06:06] Jenna Walsh: Buffer where? Like in your system?

[06:09] Naomi Feldman: Yes. The exporter has a durable queue. It’s not just in memory.

[06:13] Marcus Lin: And importantly, per destination we track a checkpoint / cursor. So if Splunk is down but S3 is fine, they’re independent.

[06:22] Marta Klein: What’s the buffer capacity? Like how long can you hold?

[06:27] Marcus Lin: In hosted and dedicated, the queue is sized so we can withstand typical downstream incidents—think hours. Exact numbers depend on tenant volume and destination count. For beta, we’re committing to a backlog SLO and we expose backlog depth estimates and “last delivered at” timestamps. For very high volume, we’ll work with you on sizing.

[06:52] Jenna Walsh: If the queue fills, do you drop events?

[06:55] Marcus Lin: We prefer explicit failure states. If we can’t deliver and the backlog is unsafe, we’ll transition the destination into a paused/degraded state and surface it in Console and via status APIs. The audit system of record still captures the events; export is a pipeline from that stream. For beta, we are not doing infinite buffering.

[07:18] Ravi Iyer: For compliance, we need evidence that audit logs are retained and immutable for some period. What’s your default retention if we don’t export?

[07:27] Naomi Feldman: In the product today, audit logs are viewable in Console for a defined retention window—today it’s 90 days for most plans, longer for enterprise contracts. For regulated customers, we typically recommend using export to your SIEM or S3 as the long-term archive.

[07:48] Ravi Iyer: So the system-of-record retention is contract-based.

[07:51] Naomi Feldman: Correct. We can include it in the enterprise terms.

[07:55] Jenna Walsh: We will export to Splunk for alerting and to S3 for archive. But you said beta includes S3 too, right?

[08:02] Fatima Noor: Yes. Initial sinks are Splunk HEC, Datadog logs intake, and S3.

[08:07] Jenna Walsh: Great. But today we’re Splunk heavy.

[08:10] Paul Nguyen: On dedupe, you said use event_id. Is it truly unique globally? Like across tenants?

[08:17] Marcus Lin: Yes—event_id is a UUID generated at emit time and is globally unique. We also include tenant/workspace identifiers so you can scope. Recommended dedupe key in Splunk is usually tenant_id + event_id, but event_id alone should be fine.

[08:35] Paul Nguyen: We can do a summary index or use “dedup event_id” in searches, but for real-time alerting we might want to use a KV store. But okay.

[08:45] Jenna Walsh: What about ordering? We have correlation rules that assume time order sometimes.

[08:50] Marcus Lin: We do not guarantee strict ordering once you go across retries and batches. We preserve emitted_at. Within a single destination, we attempt to deliver in order, but with retries you can see slight reordering.

[09:05] Marta Klein: That’s acceptable; we can use timestamp.

[09:09] Fatima Noor: Paul, on Splunk connector specifics: we have batching with limits to stay under HEC payload sizes. If any event fails schema validation, it won’t be sent. But we also have a dead-letter queue path for poison-pill events.

[09:24] Paul Nguyen: Wait, schema validation on your side? What would fail?

[09:29] Marcus Lin: For example if an internal producer starts emitting a field that violates the schema constraints, or a string is too large. We’d route that event to DLQ for operator review. We also emit metrics like “dlq_written_total.”

[09:44] Jenna Walsh: Do we get notified if things go to DLQ?

[09:47] Fatima Noor: In beta, we surface destination health: last_success_at, last_error, backlog estimate, and a state like healthy/degraded/paused. We also have SRE alerts internally. Customer-facing alert hooks are on the roadmap, but we can set up email notifications via support during beta.

[10:09] Ravi Iyer: Is the export configuration itself audited?

[10:12] Marcus Lin: Yes. Any create/update/delete of an export destination, credentials rotation, filter changes—those generate audit events as well. We did that specifically for audit trail integrity.

[10:28] Jenna Walsh: Good.

[10:30] Paul Nguyen: Can we talk about auth to Splunk HEC. Token-based obviously. Do you store it? How is it protected?

[10:38] Marcus Lin: Tokens are stored encrypted in our secrets store. Access is restricted to the export worker and control-plane service under strict RBAC. In hosted/dedicated, encryption uses KMS. For private deployments, you can bring your own KMS integration depending on setup.

[10:57] Marta Klein: For dedicated, is it in our VPC?

[11:00] Fatima Noor: Dedicated can be deployed with customer-isolated capacity. Network topology varies—some customers do VPC peering / private connectivity. For Splunk HEC, most folks still use an internet endpoint with allowlisting, but we can discuss private egress options.

[11:19] Jenna Walsh: We have strict egress controls. We can allow Splunk Cloud endpoints, but we need to know what IPs you’re coming from.

[11:27] Fatima Noor: Understood. For the hosted service, egress IP ranges can be provided per region. For dedicated, we can often provide fixed egress. I’ll take an action to follow up with our infra team if needed, but for today we can assume allowlisting is possible.

[11:46] Paul Nguyen: In Splunk Cloud, HEC endpoint is region-specific. Also, we require TLS 1.2, and we sometimes have TLS inspection. Any issues?

[11:55] Fatima Noor: TLS 1.2+ is fine. Inspection is usually fine as long as the cert chain is valid from our side. If there’s a custom CA, we’d need to support that; in private deployments it’s easier. For hosted, custom CA is not typically supported.

[12:15] Jenna Walsh: Filtering. We don’t want, like, every read-only action. Can we filter by event type and actor?

[12:22] Naomi Feldman: Yes. In the beta: filters can include/exclude by event_type, actor type/id, workspace/tenant, environment (prod/staging), and time window for replay tooling. Optional: IP/region filters—those are in the design, might be limited in the first beta drop.

[12:45] Ravi Iyer: Can you filter out user email addresses?

[12:49] Marcus Lin: Not field-level redaction via filter today. Filters are “which events,” not “edit the event.” We can discuss schema choices: we can include immutable user IDs and optionally omit email if your IdP setup provides stable IDs.

[13:07] Jenna Walsh: That’s okay.

[13:09] Paul Nguyen: For Splunk, can you set “index” in the HEC payload? We route indexes by token sometimes.

[13:15] Fatima Noor: We support specifying index in the destination config if your Splunk setup allows it. Otherwise token-level config decides.

[13:26] Paul Nguyen: Okay.

[13:28] Jenna Walsh: Operationally, how do we know it’s working? We don’t want to discover missing events three weeks later.

[13:35] Fatima Noor: You’ll have a destination health panel in Console: last delivered timestamp, last error with an error id, backlog estimate, and state. We also have a “send test event” button to validate credentials and pipeline.

[13:52] Marcus Lin: And we recommend setting up a heartbeat alert on your end: for example, expect at least one “system.health” style event per N minutes. We’re considering adding a formal heartbeat event type.

[14:07] Jenna Walsh: Is that included now?

[14:10] Naomi Feldman: Not as a formal contract item in beta. But we can discuss adding a lightweight periodic event for beta partners if it helps.

[14:20] Paul Nguyen: For test events, can you label them so we can filter out of prod dashboards?

[14:25] Fatima Noor: Yes, test events have event_type like audit.export.test or similar and include a flag “test_event=true.”

[14:34] Paul Nguyen: Nice.

[14:36] Ravi Iyer: Evidence for SOC 2: do you have controls documented around audit logs and monitoring?

[14:42] Marcus Lin: We do. We can share high-level SOC 2 statements and the relevant sections of our security whitepaper under NDA. The SIEM export itself is newer, but it’s designed to align with the “logging and monitoring” control family.

[14:59] Jenna Walsh: Great. On completeness: are there any known gaps? Like, do you miss console actions?

[15:06] Marcus Lin: Console actions are backed by APIs, so they should generate events consistently. Known limitations: for beta, we’re not doing historical backfill for all tenants. Export is primarily forward-looking from the time you enable. Replay tools can replay a time window, but there are safeguards.

[15:28] Jenna Walsh: Wait, no backfill. That’s important. We need at least from contract start.

[15:34] Naomi Feldman: Understood. For beta, we can do limited replay. For GA, broader backfill is being evaluated. Typically, customers enable export at go-live, and then their SIEM is their archive.

[15:49] Marta Klein: From an architecture standpoint, we can accept “no historical export” if the retention in your console covers the initial period. But our policy prefers centralization.

[16:03] Ravi Iyer: We would want that documented.

[16:06] Naomi Feldman: Yep. We’ll capture it in the beta terms and in the customer-facing FAQ.

[16:12] Paul Nguyen: Let’s get into Splunk failure handling. If Splunk returns 400, what do you do?

[16:17] Fatima Noor: Depends on the error. If it’s a schema issue, we don’t want to retry forever. We classify errors as auth (401/403), throttling (429), transient server (5xx), and client errors (4xx). For 429/5xx we retry with exponential backoff. For auth errors we mark destination degraded and stop sending until credentials are fixed. For “bad request,” we usually treat as non-retryable and surface error.

[16:45] Paul Nguyen: Do you drop the batch or isolate the bad event?

[16:48] Marcus Lin: We attempt to isolate. Batches are constructed from validated events. If Splunk rejects the whole batch, we can fall back to smaller batches to identify. But we don’t want retry storms.

[17:04] Jenna Walsh: Retry storms are exactly what we don’t want to cause on your side or our side.

[17:08] Marcus Lin: Agreed. That’s why we have rate limiting and circuit breakers on the exporter worker so it can’t impact the primary inference API.

[17:21] Marta Klein: That’s actually a question—does this exporter sit on the same infra as inference?

[17:26] Fatima Noor: Logically separate. It uses the control plane and a worker system. We’ve designed backpressure so it cannot steal resources from model serving.

[17:39] Jenna Walsh: Good.

[17:41] Ravi Iyer: On encryption: in transit and at rest.

[17:45] Marcus Lin: In transit to Splunk, TLS. At rest: our internal audit store is encrypted, and the queue/buffers are encrypted as well. For S3 export we support SSE-KMS (customer-managed key) in the sink configuration. For Splunk, encryption at rest is governed by your Splunk deployment.

[18:10] Paul Nguyen: For Splunk HEC, do you support sending to an HTTP proxy? We have egress proxies.

[18:16] Fatima Noor: For hosted, proxy support is limited. For private deployments, yes. For dedicated we can sometimes support outbound proxy depending on the network architecture. Let’s treat that as a follow-up item.

[18:32] Jenna Walsh: Another question: multi-tenant isolation. How do you ensure we don’t get other customers’ audit logs?

[18:38] Marcus Lin: The audit stream is partitioned by tenant/workspace, and destinations are configured per tenant. Workers operate with tenant-scoped credentials and destination IDs. We do validation at the control plane level so you can’t configure an export for another tenant. Also, export config changes are audited.

[19:00] Jenna Walsh: Okay.

[19:02] Paul Nguyen: Are there any size limits per event? Splunk HEC has some payload constraints.

[19:07] Fatima Noor: Yes. We keep audit events small—metadata only—and we batch under Splunk’s recommended thresholds. If an event is too large, it’s treated as a failure and surfaced. But it shouldn’t happen often.

[19:23] Jenna Walsh: Can you show us an example event?

[19:26] Marcus Lin: I’ll read a simplified example, and we’ll send the full schema after. Like:
- schema_version: “1.0”
- event_id: “…”
- event_type: “rbac.role_assigned”
- emitted_at: “…”
- actor_type: “user”
- actor_id: “usr_…”
- actor_display: “Jenna Walsh”
- tenant_id: “tnt_…”
- environment: “prod”
- source_ip: “…”
- resource_type: “workspace_role_binding”
- resource_id: “…”
- outcome: “success”
- request_id: “req_…”
And then a details object that’s structured, like role_name, target_user_id.

[20:06] Paul Nguyen: “details object”—is that nested JSON? Splunk can handle it, but we prefer consistent fields.

[20:12] Marcus Lin: It is structured JSON. We keep the top-level stable and the details are event-type specific, but still within a contract. The schema doc calls out required vs optional fields.

[20:26] Jenna Walsh: Schema evolution: what happens when you add fields?

[20:30] Naomi Feldman: We version the schema. Backward-compatible additions are allowed under the same major version. Breaking changes would bump the major version. Beta is v1.

[20:42] Ravi Iyer: Would you ever remove fields?

[20:44] Naomi Feldman: Not within a major version without a deprecation window. The goal is SIEM correlation stability.

[20:53] Jenna Walsh: Okay.

[20:55] Paul Nguyen: Splunk parsing: Do you set time field? We need Splunk to use emitted_at not ingestion time.

[21:02] Fatima Noor: Good catch. We include emitted_at in the payload and we recommend extracting it as _time. The setup guide has props/transforms suggestions.

[21:14] Paul Nguyen: Great.

[21:16] Jenna Walsh: Let’s talk about retention again. You said 90 days in console “most plans.” We’d want at least 180.

[21:24] Naomi Feldman: For enterprise we can do longer retention. I don’t want to promise a specific number without your contract context, but 180 is a common ask.

[21:37] Ravi Iyer: And the export stream—does it have its own retention? Like if Splunk is down for two days.

[21:44] Marcus Lin: The export queue acts as a buffer; it’s not meant to be your long-term storage. We’ll document the operational expectations. If Splunk is down for days, we’ll likely require operator intervention—pause, resume, potentially replay. We also provide replay tooling with time-window bounds.

[22:06] Jenna Walsh: Replay tooling—can a customer do that or only Redwood?

[22:10] Fatima Noor: In beta it’s primarily operator-assisted. We’re building customer-facing replay controls with safeguards. We don’t want accidental replays causing massive duplicates.

[22:24] Paul Nguyen: Right.

[22:25] Marta Klein: On private deployments, just to understand future state: if we go private, can we still do Splunk export?

[22:33] Fatima Noor: Yes, the same components run in Private. In that mode you control the network egress and secrets integration. It’s actually a better fit for strict egress and custom certs.

[22:47] Jenna Walsh: Good to know.

[22:49] Paul Nguyen: One more: Do you support multiple destinations? Like Splunk + S3 simultaneously.

[22:55] Naomi Feldman: Yes. Multiple destinations per tenant. Each destination has its own filters and state.

[23:05] Jenna Walsh: Great.

[23:07] Ravi Iyer: What about data residency. If we’re in the US, do audit logs ever leave the region?

[23:14] Marcus Lin: In hosted, audit logs are stored and processed in-region aligned with your workspace region, and export egress originates from that region. For multi-region failover, we’ll be transparent. For dedicated/private, it’s scoped to your deployment.

[23:34] Jenna Walsh: Okay.

[23:36] Paul Nguyen: Any Splunk-specific limitations in beta?

[23:40] Fatima Noor: Beta limitations: limited set of SIEM vendors—Splunk/Datadog/S3 only. No custom field mapping beyond the published schema. Limited historical backfill. Also, we’ll require you to accept at-least-once semantics and implement dedupe guidance.

[23:59] Jenna Walsh: Fine.

[24:01] Marcus Lin: Also, just to be explicit: you may see duplicates during incidents or when credentials rotate. We have guidance for rotating HEC tokens and avoiding gaps.

[24:14] Paul Nguyen: Token rotation—yeah we rotate monthly.

[24:17] Fatima Noor: Cool. We support updating the destination token; the act of changing it is audited; and the worker will detect auth failures and stop. There may be a short pause; we recommend overlapping validity windows if Splunk allows.

[24:37] Paul Nguyen: Splunk Cloud allows multiple tokens, yes.

[24:40] Jenna Walsh: Can we pause export during maintenance?

[24:44] Naomi Feldman: Yes, destination can be disabled/paused. That change is audited.

[24:52] Jenna Walsh: Great.

[24:54] Marta Klein: I’m curious, do you have any metrics like “delivery latency”? We want near-real-time for some alerts.

[25:01] Fatima Noor: We track end-to-end delivery latency. Our internal SLO targets are in the minutes range, and we alert on spikes. During normal operations it’s typically faster. For Splunk with ACK enabled, it can be slower depending on ack window.

[25:22] Jenna Walsh: Minutes is okay for audit alerts.

[25:25] Paul Nguyen: If it’s more than, say, 10 minutes consistently, our rules start breaking.

[25:31] Fatima Noor: Understood. That’s something we’ll validate in pilot and we can tune batching/ack.

[25:40] Ravi Iyer: Can you provide us the schema now? We need it for our internal review.

[25:45] Marcus Lin: Yes. We’ll send the Audit Event Schema v1 reference doc and example events.

[25:52] Jenna Walsh: And Splunk setup guide.

[25:54] Fatima Noor: Yep, both.

[25:56] Naomi Feldman: I’ll also send a short note on the beta program: how enablement works, what’s in scope, and the expected timeline.

[26:04] Jenna Walsh: Perfect.

[26:06] Paul Nguyen: One last Splunk question: Do you set HEC “host” field? We like to set host=redwood.

[26:12] Fatima Noor: We can set host to a stable identifier like “redwood-inference” or include your tenant slug. We’ll align with your preference.

[26:24] Paul Nguyen: Great.

[26:26] Jenna Walsh: Okay, I think this covers the big stuff. Next step for us is to review the schema and see if it meets our correlation needs—actor, target, request_id, ip. Then we can proceed to pilot.

[26:41] Fatima Noor: Sounds good. For pilot: we typically start with a test destination, send test events, then enable in prod environment with limited filters, and confirm ingestion and dedupe.

[26:54] Jenna Walsh: Works.

[26:55] Ravi Iyer: And I’ll need a short statement on retention and encryption for our control mapping.

[27:01] Marcus Lin: We can provide that at a high level and point to contract language.

[27:06] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[27:08] Fatima Noor: Cool. Any other questions before we wrap?

[27:12] Marta Klein: None.

[27:13] Paul Nguyen: Not right now.

[27:15] Jenna Walsh: All good.

[27:17] Fatima Noor: Great. We’ll send those two docs—schema and Splunk HEC setup guide—by tomorrow, and propose a follow-up next week.

[27:26] Jenna Walsh: Thank you.

[27:27] Marcus Lin: Thanks.

[27:28] Naomi Feldman: Thanks all.

[27:29] Meeting ended.
